fatal_errors: The proposed sluggish-diffusion, entropy-stabilization mechanism is the opposite of the target finding that diffusion is active and stability is kinetically governed by surface-energy-driven Au/Cu segregation.
The material system and intervention do not reconstruct the target: Ru-based particles and a Ru–Ni comparison replace AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles heated in situ under vacuum.

Changing from a binary alloy to a five-element alloy changes elemental chemistry, mixing energetics, and surface energies simultaneously, so the intervention does not isolate configurational entropy or lattice distortion.
The predicted retention of chemical uniformity conflicts with the observed surface segregation, melting or evaporation, particle loss, reshaping, and approximately 22% size reduction.
No cited evidence supports the quantitative claims, including the proposed two-orders-of-magnitude diffusion difference.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad question of sub-10 nm alloy stability at catalytic temperatures and offers a nominally testable HEA-versus-binary comparison. However, it largely repeats the conventional sluggish-diffusion expectation that the target study overturns. It misses the specific AuCoCuNiPt system, stepped vacuum heating, shape-dependent diffusion, low-surface-energy Au/Cu surface enrichment, and evaporation above roughly 673 K. Its binary baseline is useful operationally but compositionally confounded and therefore cannot attribute any difference specifically to entropy or lattice distortion. Post-annealing microscopy can detect segregation, but direct time-resolved diffusivity and correlated shape/composition measurements would be required to distinguish the competing mechanisms convincingly.
